name: Fatima Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Bell's Farm, which grows cabbages, carrots and leeks, and raises about two thousand turkeys for Christmas. Most of the year I'm in the fields with a hoe or on the back of the planting rig, and from October it's all turkeys. In December we pluck and dress birds from dawn till ten at night. I like the field crew, we're like a family, and I don't like my hands in January when we're cutting leeks in the frost.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been working there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years now. I stayed home with the children for twelve years, then did school cleaning, and my cousin got me in at Bell's when they were short. Martin Bell is a fair boss but I'm still the slowest on the planting rig. My husband Paolo drives a forklift at the sawmill, and we've got Sofia, who's fifteen, Luca, who's twelve, and a mortgage on a house near St Anne's church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and thank God for it. Sofia shows me the chat thing on her phone and it's clever, but I don't need it to cut a cabbage. After Mass I'd say people worry too much about machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it changes nothing, and that's mostly fine. My hours drop every January to about twenty a week, and we plan for it with Paolo's overtime at the sawmill. Every January my pay halves and every December it doubles, so my family lives on the turkeys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and ask Martin if I can learn the planting rig properly this spring. I'd keep a jar for the January money, like my mother did. Maybe I'd use Sofia's app now and then to work out the shopping, because she says it saves money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. It's a tight life, but it's ours. I'd only worry if Paolo's overtime stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Paolo's overtime stops in a January?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we ask my brother Karim for a loan till March, which I hate doing. Karim never says no. But I don't like being the sister who asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does it bother you so much to ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because family helps family, but you shouldn't lean on them every winter. My father worked two jobs so he never had to ask anyone. I'd rather work Saturdays than ask.

say: I'd say **thank God** and that people worry too much about machines.
I'd say I don't need AI to **cut a cabbage**.
think: I think nothing changes, and my **January hours** still drop to twenty.
I think my family **lives on the turkeys** in December.
do: Ask Martin to teach me the **planting rig** properly this spring.
Keep a **January jar**, like my mother did.
Use Sofia's app now and then to plan the **shopping**.
feel: She feels **steady**, worried only if **Paolo's overtime** stopped.
S0.quote: Every January my pay halves and every December it doubles, so my family lives on the turkeys.
fieldNote: Her income swings with the **seasons**, and the family plans around it.
She'd rather **work Saturdays** than ask her brother Karim for help.
Her job feels safe; the weak point is **Paolo's overtime**.

steps.text: Ask Martin to teach me the planting rig this spring
Keep a January jar with December turkey money
Use Sofia's app to plan the weekly shopping

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the offices and people at computers, not us in the field. At work I'd say Martin should be careful with any new machines. At church I'd say we should look after the young ones who lose office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I've seen the weeding robots on the television, the ones with cameras that pick out weeds. Martin says they're too dear for now. If a robot can hoe a field of carrots, Martin Bell won't need five women with hoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Martin to put me on the turkey side more, because birds still need hands at Christmas. I'd learn the planting rig well enough to drive it, since someone will need to work the machines. And I'd start saving twenty a week, even when it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little worried, under the surface. I'd keep it from the children. I'd say a rosary for Martin's bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the field crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agnieszka, who's been with the Bells for nine years and sends money home. Agnieszka's the fastest hoer on the farm, but a robot doesn't get tired. I'd worry for her more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools more, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once Martin did, maybe. If Martin showed me something on the farm computer that works, I'd learn it. I'm not first, but I'm not stupid either.

say: I'd say it's for **offices**, not people in the field.
I'd tell Martin to be careful with **new machines**.
think: I think **weeding robots** with cameras will reach the field eventually.
I think five women with hoes become **one robot**.
do: Ask Martin for more work on the **turkey side**.
Learn to drive the **planting rig** properly.
Save **twenty a week**, even when it hurts.
feel: She feels **a little worried** under the surface and hides it from the **children**.
S1.quote: If a robot can hoe a field of carrots, Martin Bell won't need five women with hoes.
fieldNote: She knows the **weeding robots** already exist and sees her hoeing as the target.
She worries more for **Agnieszka**, the fastest hoer, who sends money home.
She'd learn AI tools **once Martin uses them**, not before.

steps.text: Ask Martin for more turkey work in the autumn
Learn to drive the planting rig on my own
Save twenty a week into the January jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and the government should slow it down. At church I'd say the families need to stick together. I wouldn't go online, I'd just talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the computers do Martin's orders and his planning, which makes no difference to me. In 2031 robots weed, pick and pluck, and the field crew goes. Paolo's forklift job at the sawmill would go around the same time, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Paolo we need a plan, and we'd make one at the kitchen table that week. I'd ask Martin about working in the farm shop he keeps talking about, because people like a person behind a counter. I'd cut the car to one and ask my brother Karim if we could rent out Sofia's room to a student if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very scared. I'd pray a lot, and I'd be angry with God sometimes too. I'd be up at night thinking about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sofia and Luca?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mama and Papa will manage, and that they must study hard. Sofia wants to be a nurse, and I'd tell her yes, do it. Robots can pluck a turkey, but I'd bet my house no robot will hold my mother's hand in hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Paolo do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paolo would try for a job at the timber yard in town, but that's machines too. Paolo's proud, he'd hate to be at home. We'd both have to swallow our pride, I think.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and the government should **slow it down**.
I'd tell church families to **stick together**.
think: I think by 2031 robots **weed, pick and pluck**, and the crew goes.
I think **Paolo's forklift job** goes around the same time.
do: Make a **plan with Paolo** at the kitchen table that week.
Ask Martin about the **farm shop** counter.
Cut to **one car** and maybe rent Sofia's room to a student.
feel: She feels **very scared**, praying a lot and sometimes **angry** with God.
S2.quote: Robots can pluck a turkey, but I'd bet my house no robot will hold my mother's hand in hospital.
fieldNote: Both household jobs are **hands-on**, so both go around 2031.
She'd steer her daughter toward **nursing**, which she trusts robots won't replace.
She plans to **swallow pride** and possibly rent out a room.

steps.text: Ask Martin about working at the new farm shop counter
Sell the second car and share one with Paolo
Ask Karim about renting Sofia's room to a student
Back Sofia's plan to train as a nurse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan, so make one. At church I'd say the parish should help people find apprenticeships. I'd say it gently, because people are scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, Martin's farm shop would be built and I could be in it before the robots. Robots in 2034 means Sofia's through nursing college and Luca's nearly done with school. Five years is enough time to get my children educated before the robots take the field work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Martin to train me on the farm shop till and the butchery counter over the next two years. I'd use the AI app now and then to help with the shop's price labels, if Martin wanted. Paolo would go for his HGV licence, so he can drive timber lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but better. I can see a way through. I'd still pray every night, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you get any help from outside, from government or the parish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The parish runs a jobs club on Tuesdays, so I'd send Paolo. I'd rather an apprenticeship than benefits. Benefits are for when there's nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk the farm shop doesn't happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, Martin's been talking about it for three years. If it doesn't happen, I'd look at the supermarket in town. I'd be a shop girl again, at forty-eight.

I'd say the **parish** should help people find **apprenticeships**.
think: I think I could move to **Martin's farm shop** before the robots.
I think five years lets me get **my children educated**.
do: Train on the farm shop **till and butchery counter** over two years.
Use the AI app for the shop's **price labels**.
Push Paolo to get his **HGV licence**.
feel: She feels worried, but **better**, and can see **a way through**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to get my children educated before the robots take the field work.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **children finish training** before robots reach the field.
Her plan rests on **Martin's farm shop**, which has been talked about for three years.
She'd take an **apprenticeship over benefits**, which she sees as a last resort.

steps.text: Train on the farm shop till and butchery counter
Use the AI app to make the shop's price labels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should panic. At church I'd tell the young people to learn trades that need people. I'd say it with a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'm fifty-six and both children are grown, God willing. The field crew might be gone, but I'd have ten years to settle into the farm shop or something like it. Ten years is long enough for a field worker to become the woman behind the farm shop counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the fields for now and ask Martin to train me in the shop as soon as it opens. I'd keep saving the January jar and maybe get two months ahead for once. I'd help Sofia with her nursing applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. I'm a bit sad for the field crew. But for my family, I think we'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss, if the field work went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew, the jokes, the frost on the leeks even. It's hard, but it's honest. I'd miss being outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want from government in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help for apprenticeships, and for small farms like Bell's to stay alive. If the big farms buy all the robots and the small ones close, there's no farm shop for me to work in.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, so nobody should panic.
I'd tell young people to learn **trades that need people**.
think: I think by 2039 both **children are grown**.
I think I'd have ten years to settle into the **farm shop**.
do: Keep working the fields and ask Martin for **shop training** when it opens.
Keep the January jar and get **two months ahead**.
feel: She feels **peaceful**, though a bit **sad** for the field crew.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for a field worker to become the woman behind the farm shop counter.
fieldNote: With ten years and grown children, her own **path feels safe**.
She'd miss the **crew and the outdoors** more than the pay.
Her real worry is **small farms closing**, which would remove the shop job.

steps.text: Ask Martin for farm shop training when it opens

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Paolo and I would lose our work around the same year, with Sofia still at school. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups and help for small farms like Bell's to stay open. I'd rather learn a new trade at forty-five than take a handout, but somebody has to offer the trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the turkeys, and Christmas. Christmas at Bell's is the hardest and happiest week of my year. I'd be sad if a machine took that.

headlineQuote: I'd rather learn a new trade at forty-five than take a handout, but somebody has to offer the trade.
portrait: Fatima raised her children at home, cleaned schools, and now works the fields and turkey sheds at **Bell's Farm**.
Her pay **swings with the seasons**, and she plans January around her husband Paolo's sawmill overtime.
She uses AI **now and then** through her daughter, and would learn more once her boss does.
She becomes **alarmed** when robots come fast, but sees the **farm shop counter** as her way through.
Her faith and family guide her, and she'd take an **apprenticeship over benefits**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Paolo would lose work in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: Adult **apprenticeships** and support for **small farms** to stay open.
